questions.prompt: Explain the difference between 'some Protocol' and 'any Protocol' in Swift. In 2 to 5 sentences, describe how they differ in terms of type identity and dynamic dispatch.

rubric.criterion: Explains that some creates an opaque type where the compiler knows the single concrete type, preserving type identity and static dispatch
Explains that any creates a boxed existential type that can hold different conforming types dynamically via witness table dispatch

questions.modelAnswer: The some keyword creates an opaque type that represents one specific concrete type known to the compiler. This preserves static dispatch and type identity. In contrast, any creates a boxed existential type that can hold any conforming type at runtime. While any enables heterogeneous collections, it incurs runtime box overhead and dynamic dispatch through witness tables.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Opaque and Boxed Protocol Types

questions.prompt: Why does a function returning 'some Protocol' require all return statements to return the same concrete type? In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why returning different types causes a compiler error.

rubric.criterion: Explains that an opaque type represents one fixed underlying concrete type determined at compile time
Explains that returning different types across branches prevents the compiler from resolving a single underlying type

questions.modelAnswer: An opaque return type must resolve to a single concrete type at compile time. Even though the caller only sees the protocol interface, the compiler requires a fixed underlying type for memory layout and optimization. Returning different types from different branches prevents the compiler from determining that single type. To return different types conditionally, developers must return an existential type with any.

questions.prompt: Why does SwiftUI use 'var body: some View' instead of 'any View'? In 2 to 5 sentences, describe the performance and architectural reasons.

rubric.criterion: Explains that some View preserves the exact concrete view hierarchy type at compile time with zero box overhead
Notes that it enables SwiftUI view diffing optimizations and avoids existential container heap allocations

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI uses some View because it preserves the exact view hierarchy type at compile time without existential boxing overhead. Knowing the concrete type allows SwiftUI to perform fast, efficient view hierarchy diffing during state changes. It also avoids memory allocations and dynamic witness table dispatch that any View would introduce on every body re-evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is an existential container in Swift, and how does it store values in memory? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that an existential container includes a 3-word inline buffer, a type metadata pointer, and witness table pointers
Mentions that values larger than 3 words allocate storage on the heap, introducing memory indirection

questions.modelAnswer: An existential container is the memory structure Swift uses to represent boxed any types. It consists of a 3-word inline value buffer, a type metadata pointer, and one or more protocol witness table pointers. Small structs fit directly inside the 3-word buffer. Structs larger than 3 words allocate storage on the heap, adding memory indirection and reference counting overhead.

questions.prompt: What does 'opening an existential' mean in Swift 5.7 and later? In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how it improves ergonomics when passing existentials to generic functions.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains that opening an existential extracts the underlying concrete value from the any box at the call site
Explains that it allows passing any Protocol directly into functions expecting generic types or some Protocol without manual type casting

questions.modelAnswer: Opening an existential is a Swift feature. The compiler automatically extracts the concrete value stored inside an any container when passed to a generic function. The underlying type is bound to the function's generic parameter or some parameter. In earlier Swift versions, passing an existential caused compiler errors because the protocol did not conform to itself. Automatic unboxing makes working with existentials seamless.
